questions.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}$ and ${R}^{2}$, respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x\}$, where $x\in {R}^{3}$, is a basis of ${R}^{2}$

II. $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},4{b}_{3}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$

III. $\{{c}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The set $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{2}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}(4{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+(4{x}_{3}){b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ 4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},4{b}_{3}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},4{b}_{3}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+\frac{{x}_{3}}{4}(4{b}_{3})
$$

- Statement III is true. The set $\{{c}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ because the set consists of all the vectors from the basis $C$ written in a different order.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only".

questions.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ are bases of ${R}^{3}$ and ${R}^{2}$, respectively. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$

II. $\{-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$

III. $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. The set $\{x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}\}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the set contains vectors from another vector space.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(-2{b}_{3})+{x}_{2}(3{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}(5{b}_{2}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2{x}_{1}){b}_{3}+(3{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+(5{x}_{3}){b}_{2} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}=0 \\ 3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{-2{b}_{3},3{b}_{1},5{b}_{2}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}(3{b}_{1})+\frac{{x}_{2}}{5}(5{b}_{2})+(-\frac{{x}_{3}}{2})(-2{b}_{3})
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x\}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is false. Notice that all linear combinations of 

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\}
$$

result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{21}=0.$

- Statement III is false. Since the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of the set, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that

$$
1\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]+0\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

where the first coefficient is nonzero, so the set is linearly dependent. In general, any set that contains a zero-matrix is linearly dependent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=0\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]+(-3)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the set is not linearly independent, it can't form a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\}$ is a linearly independent set in ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$

II. $[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $\{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\}$ is a basis of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

is true if and only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]=2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{3}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]$ can't be written as a linear combination of 

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\}
$$

since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry ${a}_{21}=0:$

$$
a\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]+b\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & -a \\ 0 & 2b\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."
